#4115. TinyBuild CEO Downplays Threats of AI Game-Cloning

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

As part of the ever-growing ingress of AI slop into the gaming industry, a new threat has recently arisen in the form of AI game-cloning. In a nutshell, a user feeds footage and descriptions of a game into their toaster of choice, as well as more specific data like coding cribbed from released demos, and instructs it to make effectively the same game. The infamous recent example of this was Needle in a Haystack Simulator, a small indie game that, following its announcement, received a deluge of AI-made knock-offs that flooded the Steam store.

Developers are taking this threat very seriously. During the most recent Steam Next Fest, which was already plagued by AI slop, several indie devs decided against releasing demos out of concern that bad actors would churn out knock-offs before they could release their actual games. Some developers have admitted to receiving anonymous extortion threats, saying that if a ransom isn’t paid, the crooks will release an AI knock-off of their game before they can release the real one.

There’s even been rumors that the PC release of Grand Theft Auto 6 could be expedited just to get ahead of the proverbial slop factory that’s already churning out identical open-world crime sandbox games.

Obviously, this is a big problem, and it’s only going to get worse as AI gets smarter, but at least according to game publisher tinyBuild’s CEO Alex Nichiporchik, developers should not be afraid of these malicious duplicates. As he explained in an interview with Gamesindustry.biz, AI may be able to imitate a game’s basic aesthetics, but game feel is another matter.

If you're looking for interesting new games to keep an eye on, check out the Coolest Demos from Steam Next Fest October 2026.

As Nichiporchik points out, while AI-made knock-offs of existing or announced games may have some superficial similarities, such as setting, basic game concepts, or story beats, those elements are only part of what makes a particular game a unique experience. In fact, it’s the “experience” itself that serves as the primary differentiator, and despite its best efforts, AI can’t do much in that department.

“There's a reason that every kind of AI slop game feels the same," he explained. "It's because when you try to make something from zero, AI will multiply your skills, and zero times a thousand is still zero.”

There's a reason that every kind of AI slop game feels the same.

Nichiporchik went on to say that, rather than being afraid of having their ideas stolen, developers should consider what they can do to make their games more difficult to duplicate, primarily in how the game handles and in its core gameplay loop.

As Nichiporchik himself puts it, you could have an entire army of designers and researchers trying to completely duplicate something popular, but it just won’t have that same distinctive zing as the real thing, authentically brought to life by its original creators. It’s not unlike the number of bodies games like Fortnite or Grand Theft Auto have left in their wake as other studios try unsuccessfully to ape their formulas.

“As long as you have great game feel and a great game loop, I think you're going to be OK,” Nichiporchik assured.

Despite his assurances, Nichiporchik admitted that these AI-made games, not unlike fast food, are ubiquitous and rather obnoxious. Part of the problem is that AI knock-offs are basically trying to capitalize on the hype generated by a game’s announcement, as well as promotion like trailers or demos, stealing attention away from the genuine article or even fooling players not in the know into buying the wrong product.

Nichiporchik’s suggestion for this is to narrow the gap between announcement and release. While the standard strategy is to give the hype thrusters time to warm up and let the game accumulate wishlists and word-of-mouth, playing things close to the vest with a faster turnaround seems to work just as well.

As Nichiporchik explained, the most recent game published by tinyBuild, Probably Stolen - Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim, was announcement-ready as early as May, but tinyBuild and Questing Goose Studio decided to wait until August to announce, then release in October instead. That game’s done gangbusters despite somewhat repetitive gameplay, so it seems like the strategy worked out, and without giving bad actors nearly as much time to try to copy their notes.

Hideki Hayakawa believes that AI will never replace the human touch of creation for the video game industry.

#4114. Genshin Impact fans on PS4 only have six weeks to find another platform as support winds down with one final update

Premium in-game purchases have now been disabled on PlayStation 4, as one of Genshin's four original launch platforms prepares to get dropped in early April.

Version Luna 5 of Genshin Impact is now live, but it's a bittersweet occasion for fans of HoYoverse's breakout gacha RPG – at the very least, those who are still playing the game on PlayStation 4, which is presumably true of somebody out there.

HoYoverse announced last year that they intended to wind down support for Genshin Impact on PS4, which – alongside PC, Android, and iOS – was one of the launch platforms for the game back in 2020. And with Version Luna 5, those end days are upon us.

The game has already been delisted on the platform since last September, meaning it was no longer available for download and could only be updated by players who already had it installed. But as of today, paid purchases from the in-game store have been disabled on PS4; and in six weeks' time, on approximately April 8, Version Luna 6 will discontinue access to the PS4 version altogether.

In many ways this is unsurprising – Genshin is already available on both PS5 and Xbox Series to sate fans eager to play on console, and the PS4's hardware is increasingly struggling to keep up with this massive open-world game after more than five years of regular updates have ballooned both its file size and technical requirements.

Aptly enough, Luna 5 takes the main story action back to the nation of Mondstadt, the location where the Traveler (and, by extension, the players) took their first steps into the world of Teyvat back in September 2020. It feels like a symbolic last hurrah for the original console home of the game, as does the inclusion of a Chronicled Wish banner focussing on some of Mondstadt's most iconic (read: too old to be meta by now) 5-Star characters – namely Eula, Mona, Albedo, Klee, Diluc, and Jean.

And as the icing on the Tea Break Pancake, this banner is running alongside the long-anticipated introduction of Varka – the Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius who has been a major character in the game's lore from the very beginning, but who only became playable with today's update.

Looking ahead to that post-Luna 6 future, Genshin Impact will still be available on PS5, as well as Xbox Series consoles, PC, and mobile devices – so hopefully anyone who is still playing primarily on PS4 will find another platform they can continue the adventure on by April.

#4111. Final Fantasy 14's Evercold is Set to Be a Fascinating Social Experiment

Stephanie Watel is a writer for DualShockers. She has 3 years of experience writing about video games, from news to lists to in-depth guides.

With well over a decade now under its belt since its fateful “rebirth” in 2013, Final Fantasy XIV is one of the biggest second chance success stories in the gaming industry, and has since cemented its coveted spot in the ever-exclusive genre of MMORPGs. While its battle gameplay remains a fixture of criticism, its player community only continues to grow and the Evercold expansion is set to bring about an avalanche of groundbreaking changes to alleviate many of those criticisms at long last (hopefully).

However, if you’ve been a part of FF14’s community long enough, then it’s easy enough to realize that the game’s biggest strength has never been rooted in its divisive battle content. Where Final Fantasy 14 truly shines and ironically puts a critical spotlight on other MMOs is its social scene. Through it all, the game has retained one of the most tight-knit global playerbases, and has been praised for its incredibly welcoming social atmosphere, to the degree that some players log in simply to hang out in the game’s most beloved hubs, go to venues for community events, and everything else that makes FFXIV one of the most engaging social games to be in outside of live service IPs and the handful of other established MMOs such as World of Warcraft (which is seeing its own astronomical resurgence with its release of WoW: Forever).

All that said, the insane amount of changes that are coming to Final Fantasy 14 with Evercold’s release in February 2027 are by and large systemic in scale. This means that the way players interact and how they socialize in the game will likely change, in ways that are both subtle and not so subtle. The ripple effect it will have is all but inevitable, and it remains to be seen how exactly it will all play out, not just for Evercold but for all expansions that follow it.

For years now and from one expansion to the next, the majority of Final Fantasy 14’s social circles have organically gravitated to the game’s biggest cities, turning them into bustling hubs of conversation and commerce that seldom ever sleep, no matter your timezone. By this I’m referring to New Gridania, Ul’dah, and Limsa Lominsa, the cities that first made their grand appearance in A Realm Reborn and have since remained the places that most players return to, regardless of what expansion they’re working through or whatever other type of content that’s keeping them busy.

Subsequent expansions have since debuted some truly vibrant city hubs, from the vast, enamoring architecture in Stormblood’s Kugane to the posh rooms of Shadowbringers’s Eulmore and later the futuristic storefronts of Dawntrail’s Solution 9. However, while these places see an initial surge in player counts that linger during their respective expansion’s patch cycle, as the content surrounding it wanes and periods of “content drought” come and go, nine times out of ten, players ultimately wind up back on the benches of Limsa Lominsa or the streets of Ul’dah to congregate with their fellow Warriors of Light.

While there’s no point blank reason for why this happens with every expansion, the easy answer is that all proverbial rivers always flow back to the cities that started it all. They’re where most of the game’s seasonal events take place, for instance, to allow “sprout” players to participate alongside years-long veterans. Free Companies, or FF14’s version of guilds, are often a mix of newcomers and seasoned players, and these cities are often where they mingle outside of their respective “FC House”.

There’s the commerce side of things too, as Market Boards, which serve as the main point of contact for selling items to other players in the game, are plentiful and often only a few steps away from an aetheryte crystal teleporter. On top of that, vendors and other NPCs who teach combat, crafting, and gathering classes are easy to come by in these places, all making for a reliable hub to take care of whatever you need on the day-to-day while hanging out with your friends.

However, this dynamic that’s remained in place all these years in FFXIV may experience a sort of social earthquake with Evercold’s arrival, as the game’s character UI is set to become almost entirely self-contained when it comes to progression and upgrades. The need to seek out vendors for everything is going to shrink dramatically (at least from what we’ve been told in the Fanfest keynotes so far), which takes a vital element for these active hubs out of the equation.

If players can take their tools of progression with them on the go instead of traveling to these sources, what will that mean for not only these cities but other hubs in the game that inevitably empty out in later patch cycles? Will places like Limsa Lominsa stand firm despite these changes or will they face winds of change that happen on a subconscious level? Most of all, what does that mean for late-expac hubs like Radz-at-Han and Solution 9? Will the dynamic of how hubs function in the game as a whole experience a generational shift?

This is by and far the biggest question Evercold faces, and it will be fascinating to watch that unfold in the initial months of the expansion’s content cycle.

While the social dynamic of FF14 is potentially about to undergo its biggest evolution since the game’s inception, there is one systemic update already underway that may help smooth over the impact that has. Director Naoki (“Yoshi-P”) Yoshida and his team have been in the process of integrating the game’s massive regional data centers, which house millions of players everywhere from North America to Europe, China, Japan, and Oceania.

Up to now, those data centers have helped mesh their respective servers to help give a sense of different global “neighborhoods” that players can feel at home in. However, as the game now has such a far reach, players have since proven that friendship has no boundaries, often teaming up with Warriors of Light in entirely different regions to do content or simply hang out.

To get to another data center, however, the process was tedious to the point that it would feel even more isolating than it should have. Normally, you’d have to log out of the game entirely and facilitate a data center transfer from the log-in menu, which can take up to a few minutes. Then, if you want to jump to yet another data center that’s not your own from there, you'd have to log back out, return to your home data center, then facilitate yet another transfer to get there. Exhausting, to say the least.

Just give us the name of the second Job already!

Finally, though, that archaic process is steadily becoming history as now the NA region has merged its data centers with those in the EU, which allows players to effortlessly jump between both hubs from any main aetheryte in the game’s biggest cities. No more having to spend precious time logging out and transferring over and over. Now it’s a simple click at the aetheryte and you’re there in seconds.

Not only is this extraordinarily more convenient, such a merge is helping to dissolve that imposed isolation and help all of these “neighborhoods” feel closer together. Players no longer have to feel like they have to resort to certain servers to get the experience they want, and ultimately this could (hopefully) lead to more content participation balance across the board. That was technically the initial goal of these integrations according to Yoshi-P, to help alleviate duty queue times, but we’ll have to wait for long-term results to really get the big picture.

While so much of the game’s systemic infrastructure is getting a staggering rework for Evercold onward, one particular social feature in the game that continues to get the proverbial rug pull, sadly, is housing.

Yoshi-P did announce during the Tokyo Fanfest keynote that housing in the game is getting a budget expansion for even more plots, though they’re still actively exploring how to implement that in a more effective way that doesn’t strain the digital space they have for it. Whether that’s creating “hidden” plot areas or more districts remains to be seen, and we’ll have to wait until after Evercold’s debut to find out the result.

While it’s always nice to have more room for players to settle and customize their home away from home, the hard truth is that FFXIV’s housing system remains an inconvenient mess with no indication of when we could potentially see the systemic change it so desperately needs. Over the years, the game has dealt with creating too much artificial scarcity for housing, turning it into far more of a privilege than it should be in a global MMORPG.

While it still should be earned through personal progression of the game, housing should be a guaranteed reward for your efforts. Forcing players to endure weeks or months of countless lottery drawings for a particular plot is equal parts exhausting and demeaning. On top of that, once you finally have a plot to put your name on, you can only keep it so long as your subscription remains active. Should you dare to not log in for more than a month or so, you face the prospect of a digital eviction, your purchased furnishings tossed to the curb, and a pity deposit back for your troubles.

It’s a glaring reality of how the game has chosen to approach housing from the get-go, and how those decisions have led it down a path that it can’t seem to escape or fix in an effective manner. Instead, it’s more plots to placate the masses, the option to manipulate the amount of interior space for an additional gil fee, and a long overdue unlock on the ability to “float” furnishings. These are nice additions, but I’ve long viewed FF14’s housing situation from the bigger picture.

Ultimately, I think it comes down to the desire to make housing genuinely feel like a neighborhood you can actively walk around in rather than making it entirely instanced like other games do. Trying to honor that immersion is commendable, but when it comes at the cost of depriving countless players of the opportunity to experience that based on a skewed luck system, then what is the point in the end?

All that said, I’m not without the hope that things could still change in the future for housing. Rather, it could very well be that it needs its own expansion to pull it off, just as the game’s done with its graphic overhaul in Dawntrail and now the gameplay overhaul in Evercold. Or perhaps, this is the way it truly needs to be in Final Fantasy 14 in terms of the game’s social dynamic. Maybe losing our digital neighborhoods to instanced housing isn’t the answer. Whatever it could turn out to be, to truly strengthen the game’s social sphere, housing needs to be something attainable for everyone, not a privileged few.

Final Fantasy XIV’s combat has been an ongoing point of discussion, criticism, praise, and everything in between. However, in the years of Dawntrail’s patch cycle, the criticism reached a fever pitch in regards to the game’s growing lack of job identity and how said jobs haven’t seen much of a systemic update at all since A Realm Reborn. It had gotten to the point that the future of FFXIV had reached a questionable stage, and that if these ongoing issues weren’t addressed then the MMO could see a tragic downturn sooner rather than later.

With that, Evercold is set to bring about a slew of long-awaited changes to battle content, pretty much from top to bottom. Virtually every aspect of combat in the game is set to get some degree of change, along with entirely new additions such as the already widely praised Gauntlet of Power. Meanwhile, existing content such as Alliance Raids are getting dissected and reworked to hopefully better fit modern playstyles where time is more precious and content needs to be more inherently beneficial to players.

These changes are yet another factor in the equation that will undoubtedly affect how players will team up and work together in a post-Evercold setting versus the traditional methods that have driven the game for years. Having more flexibility in playstyle and more diversity in the types of battle content that are available are definitely net positives for FF14, and it will be interesting to see how that subsequently helps the social aspect of the game evolve in the months and years to come.

#4109. The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin may be your next anime gacha obsession, with a hint of Ghibli, and this latest trailer may be what sells you on it

There's another free-to-play action RPG very much on the horizon. Will this be the one to win you over?

It seems like we’re getting one of these every few months, but the world of mobile action RPGs that look like the games that, just a few years back, were only possible on consoles is expanding with another new entry.

Netmarble, a studio and publisher known for its free-to-play games on mobile and PC, recently unveiled the launch date for The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin, its next major release that’s very much coming for the Genshin Impact crowd.

The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin is an open-world action RPG based on the world of The Seven Deadly Sins anime and manga. The game takes place in the world of Britannia, which looks similar to the way it does in the anime.

That said, the story of the game is not based on the anime or manga, Instead, it’s an original story set in the universe of the show. You play as Prince Tristan of the Kingdom of Liones who must find a way to bring order back to Britannia.

The gameplay should be familiar to anyone who played a free-to-play action RPG in the last decade. It features action combat, a roster of diverse heroes that you assemble to form teams, and a large pretty world to explore where you’ll also get to meet new characters.

Speaking of which, while Origin has its own original story, expect to be teaming up with characters from the series - some of whom wouldn't be able to meet naturally. You can thank the game's multiversal story for that.

Beyond all the serious business of saving the world and battling monsters, The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin also has a cozy, relaxing side. You’ll be able to fish, cook, forage and take on the beauty of the world with your pals.

#4108. The Blood Of Dawnwalker Just Got A Free 1.2 Update, Adding New Game Plus

The Blood of Dawnwalker is one of the year's biggest, most ambitious games, and the developers over at Rebel Wolves have done a good job cleaning up bugs and performance issues in the weeks since launch. Today, that trend continued; the new 1.2 update is out now on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC, and it adds New Game Plus.

The new mode is uniquely ideal for a game like Dawnwalker. The narrative is very player-driven, whether it has to do with your literal dialogue options, your ability to manage your vampiric hunger, or the order you complete quests, and all of these elements can cause your experience to vary wildly. It makes sense, then, that players would want to jump back in to try things again and see what might happen if the game is played differently, and New Game Plus allows them to do that while keeping combat fresh.

According to the update notes on the Dawnwalker website, "NG+ unlocks after you complete the game’s Epilogue and lets you experience the story again while keeping your progress – mainly your character level, skills, and inventory." You don't gain access to these skills until you complete the prologue, however, which marks the adventure's proper start.

The new mode will also rebalance the world's level scaling. In the base game, certain areas are much harder than others, but in New Game Plus, all enemies will rise in power to match your level, meaning you can explore the world in whatever order you want. On that note, the level cap has also been raised to 100, and protagonist Coen can collect new, more powerful versions of weapons marked with an "NG+" label.

That's basically everything in this update. Rebel Wolves also added some slight tweaks to combat in the base game and adjusted some geometry in the open world, but the main focus here was New Game Plus. This is in contrast to the 1.1 update, which added a much wider suite of bug fixes and made the game run more smoothly.

#4107. 9 Best Tech Parodies in GTA 6

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

The Grand Theft Auto series tends to be a parody of real life, with there being loads of satirical comedy woven throughout the many fibers of each game. This trend continues in Grand Theft Auto 6, with there being loads of hilarious parodies of well-known companies, television shows, radio broadcasts, and even tech.

Tech plays a big role in the game, as you use your phone for many things, such as ordering a ride on the RydeMe app, or even bucking yourself using the aptly named BuckMe app.

You are going to be relying on a lot of tech companies throughout GTA 6, so it is obvious that there will be a number of jokes surrounding them.

Texting plays a huge role in real life. After all, you text your friends, family members, and even coworkers about what is going on in your life. The same is done in GTA 6, and the game captures texting quite well, with both protagonists texting one another and various people about jobs.

While you may normally use the popular WhatsApp application to get your fill of communication, the people of GTA 6 use a slightly different app called WhatUp. This is a very obvious parody of WhatsApp, with a name that is almost identical.

Even the user interface is almost identical, with it featuring a very minimalist style showing the avatar or profile picture of each contact next to the messages.

Amazon is a go-to tech and shipping company for many people nowadays. While we all may complain about capitalism, there is no denying the convenience of having everything at your fingertips through the use of an app that has next-day shipping.

In GTA, the citizens of Leonida are using a slightly different company that is a clear parody of Amazon, and it is called Sahara. You can find boxes scattered around that mimic the exact shipping tape used by the company, the logo is very similar, and there is even Sahara Mirage, which is meant to be a parody of Amazon Prime.

Money makes the world go ‘round in real life, and it especially makes the world go ‘round in GTA 6. You are on a constant mission to collect money in the game, which in a way mimics real life. Anyway when you are handling money in real life, you might use a banking app, or you might use CashApp or Venmo.

GTA 6 has an app that parodies these real-life tools and it is called BuckMe - a hilarious name that has various uses, such as when you give yourself money, which is called bucking yourself.

This app is the go-to banking app that you get at the start of the game because you can’t afford to open a real checking account and it is just perfect.

In typical Rockstar fashion, get ready for some parodies of popular websites and mobile apps.

Did you know that you can play games within GTA 6? Odds are you probably did, and it is thanks to Cal. He so graciously installs the new JoyStation in Jason’s home early in the game, allowing you to catch up on your gaming within your game.

The JoyStation is an obvious parody of the PlayStation 5, with the console looking almost identical to the real-life system you are probably playing GTA 6 on. Even the user interface looks extremely close to the real-life version.

The console isn’t just for looks, as it can be used to play some real games, with some of them even being easter eggs for real-life movies and games.

When you need to get around the city in real life, you either rely on your car to get you from point A to point B, or you rely on someone else’s car. This can come in the form of a ride that you hire via a rideshare app like Lyft or Uber.

Just like in real life, you can get from point to point in GTA 6 by using the convenient ridesharing app aptly called RydeMe. It even comes complete with a Y instead of an I so you know it was made by the tech bros in Silicon Valley.

The app is great, as it lets you fast travel around the city. If only you could skip the unwanted conversation with the driver in real life. At least the prices match up with the inflated real-life equivalent.

A new Grand Theft Auto 6 leak has finally shown Lucia's gameplay and opening chapter, confirming that Uber/Lyft parodies are in the game.

Doomscrolling has become the norm lately, as apps like YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok all offer short-form content that you can easily digest and swipe away. Luckily, GTA 6 hasn’t gone that far… yet.

While you can’t doomscroll reels in GTA 6, you can flip through tons of posts thanks to the improved Snapmatic app. This app made an appearance in GTA 5, as it was used to take pictures.

Now, you can use it to scroll through countless posts about how we got something else before RAC 7. You can even read the comments, and those are something else entirely, so be prepared.

Dating in real life has been boiled down to a few different dating apps, but if you are looking to hook up with someone, you are probably going to use Tinder. Of course, you could try FarmersOnly, but to each their own.

Sadly, you can’t get the experience of using a dating app in GTA 6, but you can help out Cal. Early in the game, you get to see the in-game version of Tinder, as Cal hands you his phone and you get to swipe right or left on various dating profiles.

The app is pretty accurate to the real-life equivalent, complete with cringy profiles, horrible pictures, and people with way too high of standards.

There has been a rise of people who are vaping, and as someone who used to vape all the time, it is sad to see how much it has grown at times. Vaping has infected the world of Leonida as well, but one in particular that is worth pointing out is Manifestick.

This hilarious parody is meant to replace anxiety pens and mock those who wear a vape on a leash around their neck, as there are women who use them like they are addicted to them.

Oh wait, that is because they are addicted. You can discover that these vape pens are laced with cocaine, making them not so friendly and very addictive like the real-life nicotine infused sticks.

Cryptocurrency is everywhere nowadays. There are people who swear on Bitcoin, and we see a meme coin pop up almost every day. We have all heard stories of people being scammed because someone did a rug pull.

Throughout the game, you will interact with a company called AudaCity, and there is even a character named Papa Audacity. This company is creating DacityCoin, and you are meant to promote it with Redbull-style stunts that push the coin’s value up.

The protagonists even call out how the coin is a scam, but that doesn’t mean you can’t get in on the ground floor and be one of the few who profits off of everyone else’s losses.

Like many games, Grand Theft Auto 6 is full of easter eggs for you to discover. These are some of the best Leonida has to offer.

#4106. Shopify Rebellion Black beat Xora 2-0 in opening VCT Americas Kickoff qualifier match

Shopify Rebellion Black opened the North America Qualifier Playoffs with a 2-0 win over Xora Esports. The non-partner organisation is now one win from the playoffs that decide a guaranteed São Paulo Kickoff place.

The best-of-three Group Stage meeting with Xora began at 00:10 UTC on Saturday 21 November, opening Shopify Rebellion Black’s VCT Americas Kickoff: North America 2027 campaign.

The result counts for more because Shopify Rebellion is now outside Riot’s partnership system. The organisation was one of the Americas sides that said it had not been chosen for the 2027-2028 partnership programme, Sheep Esports reported. Cloud9, ENVY, M80, FlyQuest and LYON were also on that list. Riot now has eight partner teams in each of its four regions.

The Swiss Stage runs from 20 to 22 November 2026. Every match is best of three. Two wins send a team through to the playoffs, and two losses knock it out. The eight teams left after the Swiss phase move into a double-elimination bracket played over six competition days, with the playoffs set for 1 to 6 December. The event is listed as an online, A-Tier Riot Games qualifier for 16 teams.

Shopify Rebellion Black’s next opponents are Oafs, who also won their opening match 2-0, against QoR. Both teams are therefore one win from the playoffs. Oafs already have a record against Xora. They knocked them out of the Qualifier 1 bracket on 8 November with a 2-1 win. Xora had still reached the Qualifier Playoffs by finishing joint third in the 512-team North America Qualifier 1.

Across 83 rated matches, Shopify Rebellion Black hold a 59-24 record. Before this event their most recent series was a 2-3 defeat to 2GAME Esports at the VCL Americas Last Chance Qualifier 2026. Earlier in that event they had beaten 2GAME Esports 2-1 and Contra 2-0.

The organisation’s second line-up had a harder start. Shopify Rebellion Gold lost 0-2 to Maryville University. Several of the other organisations left out of the partnership programme won their first matches. Cloud9 beat counterfeit 2-0, Team Envy beat Yellow Dragon Gaming 2-0 and FlyQuest edged Masterclass 2-1. Elsewhere, Winthrop University beat SaD Esports 2-0 and YFP Gaming beat Wildcard 2-1.

The prize for coming through the bracket is a place in São Paulo. Riot will stage the 2027 VCT Americas Kickoff in Brazil. Its eight Partner Teams get direct entry. Non-partner teams can win four places: one guaranteed slot each for North America, Brazil and Latin America, plus one for the Americas Last Chance Qualifier. For a non-partner side, a later run to Masters would be worth a fixed US$200,000 and a place at Champions US$400,000, Dot Esports reported. The regional Kickoff events are due to start on 14 January 2027 and run until 7 February 2027.

#4103. Marathon may actually have a shot as Server Slam hits it big on Steam

Marathon's latest public open weekend has kicked off, and it looks like enough people have showed up to play it.

Things are officially looking better for Marathon. The game’s Server Slam, essentially an open beta that’s freely available everywhere, has kicked off. This is the last chance for anyone curious about Bungie’s next big game to play it before it officially goes on sale next week.

Considering how unpopular the game has been throughout its development, and judging by the feedback from earlier closed beta tests, the turnout for the Server Slam is definitely encouraging.

The Marathon Server Slam has been online for a little over 12 hours on Steam, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. Only one of those platforms shares player numbers, of course, but it's enough to offer some visibility into how popular the test has been.

Immediately after servers went live, Marathon shot up the Steam most played charts. The game quickly achieved a peak of 143,621 concurrent players (via SteamDB), which is very respectable. Given that the Server Slam will be available for the entire weekend, there’s every chance the numbers will go up.

These figures are particularly encouraging when you look at Arc Raiders, the current top dog in the extraction shooter space, and the game that stole Marathon’s thunder last year when the two of them were being promoted by their publishers. Marathon, of course, got delayed out of 2025, which allowed Arc Raiders to launch first. It, of course, ended up proving that extraction shooters can be mainstream hits.

Like Marathon, Arc Raiders hosted its own server slam just a few days before its launch. That open test attracted 189,668 concurrent players at its peak, which is not that far off from Marathon’s so far.

Assuming positive word of mouth continues, more players are bound to jump in over the weekend and perhaps get Marathon to match or even exceed Arc Raiders’ record. At any rate, this is good news for beleaguered Bungie and points to what could be a big launch.

#4102. CD Projekt Red CEO Puts Ambition Ahead of Budget in Witcher and Cyberpunk Development

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

It’s no secret that Grand Theft Auto 6 was not a cheap game to make, to put very, very mildly. While Rockstar has not publicly disclosed the game’s precise internal price tag, rumors have circulated that it’s somewhere in the billions, and considering the sheer scope and complexity of the game’s world, I don’t think that theory is an unreasonable one.

Considering the amount of cash that undoubtedly went into GTA 6’s development, which has now been followed by immense success and landmark profits for Rockstar and Take-Two, also in the billions, something of a new precedent has been established for the AAA gaming sector. Arguably, it's not a great one: if you keep pouring massive stacks of cash into your game, it’ll magically make billions of dollars forever.

Obviously, this is completely untrue, but that doesn’t stop people from wondering, especially as far as other power-player devs are concerned. For example, CD Projekt Red, developer and publisher of landmark IPs like The Witcher and Cyberpunk, has invested its fair share of capital into its works. However, according to its CEO, Michal Nowakowski, the budget of CDPR’s titles is secondary to their ambitions and goals.

Rockstar is known for putting insane levels of detail into their games, but here is how they are going above and beyond with GTA VI.

During CD Projekt Red’s Q3 2026 Earnings Call, the audio of which was posted to the company’s official YouTube channel, Nowakowski was asked his opinion on the “technological and qualitative leap” between Grand Theft Auto 5 and 6, and in turn, how those landmark advancements might inform CDPR’s developmental philosophy going forward, particularly with in-development Witcher and Cyberpunk titles.

Nowakowski acknowledged the major precedent that has been put forth by Rockstar through GTA 6 through the industry at large, but he also clarified that, in spite of that game’s success, he and his company don’t make their games just to compete with those produced by another.

“If anything happened as a result of GTA 6, it's always great to see games like that because they show you how much cool stuff can be done. That's for sure an inspiration in many ways for our developers.”

He and his company don’t make their games just to compete with those produced by another.

When asked how GTA 6’s developmental scope might affect budget expectations for upcoming games, Nowakowski stressed that Witcher and Cyberpunk are not “budget-driven developments,” and while he is always conscious of how much money it costs to make top-shelf games, it’s not really conducive to a product’s health to be constantly keeping the budget in mind during the developmental process.

“They are ambition-driven developments and money is important, the budgets are not indefinite, that's not what we're saying. And honestly, that philosophy has not changed for us because of GTA 6.”

The obvious problem with expecting new games, even AAA ones, to have comparable budget and scope to GTA 6 is that not every game is GTA 6, nor is every developer Rockstar. Not everyone is going to have that kind of raw spending power available, and certainly, not everyone has access to the kind of prestige IP with a baked-in fanbase like GTA.

Overbloated budgets for AAA games have already been a consistent problem and talking point for at least a decade now, with players regularly complaining that too much money is spent on making games look visually and technologically impressive without making the core experience any better. This ends up dragging out development cycles and bleeding companies dry, not to mention subjecting developmental staff to intense crunch. Heck, lest we forget, GTA 6 took over a decade itself to come out, and was delayed twice.

While it is heartening to hear Nowakowski’s proclamation of ambition over budget, it is very difficult to predict where the AAA sector is going now that the shadow of GTA 6 is looming over it. Personally, I’d like to believe that players won’t expect every new game they play to also be GTA 6-tier, but, well…

GTA VI will be one of the biggest video game releases in our lifetimes, and it will be talked about for years to come.

#4100. Civilization Developer Firaxis Lays Off A Third Of Its Staff

Firaxis, the studio behind the Civilization series, has laid off around 60 employees, representing a third of its staff. The report comes from Bloomberg’s Jason Schreier.

In a statement provided to Bloomberg by a spokesperson from 2K, a subsidiary of Firaxis' owner, Take-Two, “Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength—designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years. As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis.”

In addition to the 60 affected staffers, Firaxis studio head Heather Hazen is also departing. Bloomberg also reports, via anonymous Firaxis employees speaking to the outlet, that the studio is working on an unannounced XCOM game that has had a challenging development, with the team recently missing an important development milestone. This project, if it releases, will be the first Firaxis-developed XCOM game since XCOM: Chimera Squad in 2020.

Firaxis’ most recent release is Civilization VII, which launched in February 2025 to favorable reviews but initially "slow" sales, according to Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick last August.  The game currently has a Mixed reception on Steam after Firaxis spent the last year updating the game to address player complaints. Before Civilization VII, Firaxis shipped Marvel's Midnight Suns in 2022, another critically well-received game that failed to meet sales expectations.

#4099. The Sims 4 is getting paid mods, and a new in-game currency to pay for them

The Sims 4 is about to launch a couple of major initiatives that may not exactly be what players have been looking for.

The Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era. Developer Maxis announced The Sims Maker Program, and The Sims 4 Marketplace - two new destinations to publish, and discover new add-on content.

The two new features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17. PlayStation and Xbox players will receive them over the next couple of months, which is very much in line with how other franchises have rolled out their own paid mods systems.

The Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it. The content they create will end up on the Marketplace, where other players can browse it, and pay for it if they want to use it in their game.

Created content will be available across all platforms. All previous packs The Sims 4 players should be familiar with will move to the Marketplace, too: once the feature launches, this is where you’re going to find Expansion Packs, Game Packs, Stuff Packs, Kits, and other official additions created by Maxis.

Alongside this, the game is also introducing a new virtual currency - Moola - which is what you’re going to use to purchase Maker Packs, as well as Sims 4 Kits in the Marketplace. A portion of your purchase will go to the creator (roughly 30%) of what you buy.

It is worth noting, however, that you’ll still be able to buy Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs without having to purchase Moola, or go through the Marketplace. Kits are the only items that will no longer be available on the existing PC/console storefronts. Moola comes in the usual denominations you’ve seen a hundred items in other games’ in-game shops.

In order to start creating custom content and publishing it on the Marketplace, you’ll need to first be accepted into the program. Once that’s done, you’ll be able to directly publish your content on the Marketplace.

In the blog post announcing the new features, Maxis said that creators will have control over the price of their content, and how it's packaged. These are referred to as Maker Packs, which can include Create-a-Sim or Build/Buy items.

You can apply to become a Maker from March 5. Once accepted, you’ll also get access to the Maker Suite, which is what you’re going to use to test your work to ensure it runs smoothly on the different platforms, and eventually publish it.
